How to Create Custom Commands in OpenCode

Save a Markdown prompt as .opencode/commands/check-file.md, then type /check-file followed by your arguments in OpenCode’s terminal UI. For a command you use in every project, put its file in the global commands folder. In OpenCode 2.4.1, opencode run sends slash text directly as a prompt.

  1. Create a Markdown command
  2. Pass arguments to the template
  3. Check which command loads
  4. Use a command from a script
  5. See the tested expansions

Where are you using the command?

Create commandCheck CLI optionsCheck file scope

Create an OpenCode slash command

Check opencode --version. In an OpenCode 2 project, save this as .opencode/commands/check-file.md. Use a project without private data for the first run.

---
description: Review a file and report test gaps
agent: plan
---

Review $1 for $2. List findings before proposing changes.

Open OpenCode in the project and enter this in its prompt composer.

/check-file src/demo.ts "error handling"

The Markdown body supplies the prompt template. Use frontmatter for metadata such as the label and agent. To define the same sort of command in opencode.jsonc, add an entry under commands with a template value. Keep a unique name while testing.

Pass arguments and attach files

  • $ARGUMENTS inserts the full argument string, including the quotes as entered.
  • $1, $2 and later positions use parsed arguments. Quotes group words. The highest position in the template also gets the remaining arguments, so $2 in the example can include all remaining focus words.
  • If the template has no placeholders, OpenCode appends the arguments after a blank line.

A path argument inserts text. To attach the file itself, use the composer’s attachment action. The official commands documentation also describes shell blocks, which run locally during expansion outside the agent tool permission flow. Use a text-only template for this check and keep untrusted arguments out of shell blocks.

When an OpenCode command is missing or uses old text

  1. Check the workspace. A global Markdown command normally lives under ~/.config/opencode/commands/, while a project command lives in .opencode/commands/. Run opencode debug paths to locate the current profile’s config folder.
  2. Check the Markdown extension and the name. For example, team/check-file.md inside commands/ becomes /team/check-file.
  3. Look for the same name in the global directory and project configuration. In our test, the project Markdown command won over a global Markdown command with the same name. Try a unique command name if you are unsure which one OpenCode selected.

For other configuration overrides, check which OpenCode config files are loaded.

Why a slash command does not expand in opencode run

In OpenCode 2.4.1, opencode run --help lacks the older --command flag. Our CLI test rejected that flag. Passing /team/review src/demo.ts as the message sent those literal characters. To automate the prompt with the CLI, pass the expanded prompt text yourself. For an integration that needs the actual command definition, use the documented OpenCode server command API on the intended session.

Check the installed version before copying an example from V1. An accepted server request means the command was submitted. Check the session or output to confirm what ran.

What OpenCode 2.4.1 sent for each template

TemplateObserved prompt
Nested Markdown with $1 and $2Used the project file, grouped quoted words and kept the rest of the focus phrase.
JSON command with $ARGUMENTSKept the original argument string and quotes.
JSON command without placeholdersAppended the file path after a blank line.

We called the command API on a local authenticated OpenCode server in a temporary macOS arm64 project. A loopback provider captured the actual expanded text and returned a fixed reply. The test measured expansion, project selection and the CLI behavior. Terminal UI steps are from the documentation. Download the command checks.
